title: THE UNTOLD STORY OF PRISCILLA
paragraphs: The Woman Who Quietly Helped Shape the Early Church
And sometimes the people who change the world are not the ones standing behind pulpits, sitting on thrones, or having books named after them.
Sometimes they are the ones opening their homes.
And disappearing from the spotlight before anyone notices what they just accomplished.
Priscilla was one of those people.
Even fewer understand why the Holy Spirit preserved her name in Scripture.
Yet hidden within the pages of the New Testament is the remarkable account of a woman whose influence quietly reached some of the most important leaders of the early Church.
A woman who risked her life for the Gospel.
A woman who helped disciple one of Christianity's greatest preachers.
A woman whose ministry challenges modern believers to rethink what true spiritual influence really looks like.
This is the untold story of Priscilla.
And before it ends, you may find yourself asking a question that changes everything:
What if the greatest ministry is not the one everyone sees?
What if the greatest ministry is the one Heaven remembers?
The First Time We Meet Priscilla
The first appearance of Priscilla occurs in Acts 18.
Luke introduces her alongside her husband Aquila.
"They found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla..." (Acts 18:2)
In ancient culture, husbands were normally mentioned first.
Yet throughout the New Testament, Priscilla's name frequently appears before Aquila's.
This has caused biblical scholars for centuries to ask why.
Some suggest she may have come from a prominent Roman family.
Others believe she possessed exceptional spiritual maturity.
Still others think her ministry role was especially influential.
While certainty is impossible, one thing is undeniable:
The Holy Spirit repeatedly preserved her name in a position rarely granted to women in ancient historical records.
That should make us pay attention.
Priscilla and Aquila were not living comfortable lives when Paul met them.
The Roman historian Suetonius records that Emperor Claudius expelled many Jews from Rome around AD 49.
Many believers today know that feeling.
Priscilla understood what it felt like to have life interrupted.
Yet what looked like disaster became divine positioning.
Had Rome never expelled them, they might never have met Paul.
And if they never met Paul, countless lives might have remained untouched.
Sometimes God is working through the very disruption we are praying Him to remove.
Acts 18 tells us Paul lived and worked with Priscilla and Aquila because they shared the same trade.
Literally, one who makes tents or leather shelters.
Conversations about Christ while earning a living.
Just faithful believers doing ordinary work for an extraordinary Kingdom.
Many modern Christians underestimate the holiness of ordinary faithfulness.
Yet Priscilla reminds us that some of God's greatest work happens in workshops, offices, kitchens, classrooms, construction sites, and living rooms.
Before she ever taught anyone publicly, she served God faithfully in everyday life.
The Church in Her Living Room
One detail about Priscilla's life appears repeatedly.
"Greet also the church in their house."
The word "ἐκκλησία" (ekklēsia) became the New Testament term for church.
But originally it referred to a gathered assembly.
The Church was not a building.
And Priscilla opened her home so those people could gather.
Hosting Christians could attract unwanted attention.
Yet she opened her doors anyway.
Priscilla created space where ministry could happen.
The Day She Corrected a Famous Preacher
Then comes one of the most fascinating moments in the entire New Testament.
Acts 18 introduces a brilliant preacher named Apollos.
"He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately."
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say they humiliated him.
It does not say they embarrassed him publicly.
It does not say they attacked him.
It says they took him aside.
The Greek phrase "ἀκριβέστερον" (akribe steron) means "more accurately" or "more precisely."
Priscilla helped strengthen a gifted preacher's understanding of truth.
And because she did, Apollos went on to become one of the most influential Christian leaders in the first century.
A woman many Christians barely remember helped disciple a preacher many Christians still study.
What if some of the most important people you will ever influence are not famous yet?
What if God places future leaders in your path?
Will you care enough to help them grow?
Risking Her Life for the Gospel
Paul later writes these astonishing words:
The Greek literally suggests exposing one's neck to danger.
We are never told exactly what happened.
Priscilla was willing to suffer for Christ.
She was willing to suffer for God's servants.
She was willing to place herself in danger for the Kingdom.
What are we willing to risk?
What are we willing to sacrifice?
How valuable is the Gospel to us?
Because for Priscilla, Jesus was worth everything.
The Forgotten Heroes of the Kingdom
There is no recorded sermon from Priscilla.
No biblical book bears her name.
No miracle is directly attributed to her.
No chapter centers exclusively on her story.
But her influence echoes for centuries.
Perhaps that is why her story matters so much today.
We live in a culture obsessed with visibility.
"And your Father who sees in secret will reward you."
Much of her work happened behind closed doors.
What Her Story Means for Us
They wonder whether their service matters.
Priscilla's story answers with a resounding yes.
The Kingdom is built not only by those standing on stages.
It is built by faithful servants whose names may never trend on earth but are known in Heaven.
And perhaps that is the greatest lesson hidden inside the story of Priscilla.
You do not have to be famous to be fruitful.
You do not have to be visible to be valuable.
You do not have to stand in front of crowds to change eternity.
Sometimes the people who change the world are simply the people who make room for God to work.
Maybe you are tempted to quit.
The same God who saw Priscilla sees you.
The same God who used Priscilla can use you.
And the same Jesus who transformed the Roman world through hidden servants is still doing it today.
One day, many of Heaven's greatest heroes will be people earth barely noticed.
